name: Surkanda Devi Temple
summary: Surkanda Devi near Kanatal is the Himalayan Shakti Peetha associated with the head of Goddess Sati — a major Devi seat of Tehri Garhwal.
famousFor: Shakti Peetha — Head of Sati · Kanatal ridge shrine
mythology: The Shakti Peetha cycle rests on the Puranic narrative of Daksha’s yajna, Sati’s self-immolation, and Shiva’s grief-stricken tandava. Vishnu’s Sudarshana chakra is said to have dismembered Sati’s body; where each portion fell, a peetha of the Goddess arose.

mythologySignificance:
The Shakti Peetha cycle rests on the Puranic narrative of Daksha’s yajna, Sati’s self-immolation, and Shiva’s grief-stricken tandava. Vishnu’s Sudarshana chakra is said to have dismembered Sati’s body; where each portion fell, a peetha of the Goddess arose.

Surkanda Devi Temple at Near Kanatal, Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand is counted among these seats in widely followed pilgrimage lists. Tradition in the popular 51-peetha pilgrimage enumeration associates this seat with the Head of Sati · Kanatal ridge shrine of Goddess Sati. Scriptural enumerations differ (often 51, 52, or 108); Devi / Kalika Purana traditions and later Pithanirnaya-style lists underpin how pilgrims map this geography today.

Goddess Surkanda Devi (Kali / Sati) is worshipped here as the living Shakti of the peetha — fierce or gentle according to local form, yet always as the mother who sanctifies place through the Sati–Shiva story.
localBeliefs:
At Surkanda Devi Temple, priests and elders retell the peetha association (Head of Sati · Kanatal ridge shrine) as the reason devotees undertake long journeys for darshan of Goddess Surkanda Devi (Kali / Sati). Navaratri, local jatras, and family kuladevi vows intensify belief that the Goddess of this seat answers specifically here.

Offerings, colours of flowers or cloth, and animal-sacrifice customs (where still practised under temple rules) vary by region — pilgrims are taught to follow only what the local peetha permits.

Because peetha lists themselves vary, local tradition at the shrine is treated as authoritative for ritual detail, while the pan-Indian Sati narrative supplies the shared mythological frame.
